result.summary: Pluto carries off Persephone with Zeus's help, and Demeter searches for her, comes to Eleusis, and tries to make Celeus's child immortal. After Triptolemus is given wheat to sow, Persephone eats a pomegranate seed and must spend a third of each year with Pluto.

scenes.title: Persephone Carried Off
scenes.summary: Pluto, helped by Zeus, secretly abducts Persephone. Demeter searches the earth, learns the truth from the people of Hermion, and leaves heaven in anger.
scenes.stakes: Demeter risks losing her daughter forever; Persephone is taken from the upper world.

scenes.title: Demeter at Eleusis
scenes.summary: Demeter arrives at Eleusis disguised, is made to smile by Iambe, and nurses Metanira's child Demophon in the fire. Praxithea cries out on seeing him, the child is consumed and the goddess reveals herself.
scenes.stakes: Demophon's life, and the chance of making him immortal, is lost when the nurse is discovered.

scenes.title: Triptolemus and the Wheat
scenes.summary: Demeter gives Triptolemus a dragon chariot and wheat to sow across the earth. Other authors give him different parents.

scenes.title: The Pomegranate Seed
scenes.summary: Persephone is made to eat a pomegranate seed, Ascalaphus testifies against her and is buried under a rock, and Persephone must spend a third of each year with Pluto.
scenes.stakes: Persephone's freedom to return permanently to her mother; Ascalaphus is punished.

alias_notes.explanation: Persephone is also called Kore, the Maiden.

analysis.text: The passage explains the seasons through Persephone's divided year and shows Demeter's grief, anger and gift of grain.
It links myth to Eleusis, the Eleusinian Mysteries and the ritual jesting at the Thesmophoria festival.

legacy.text: The myth of Demeter and Persephone became a classic explanation of the seasons and inspired much later art and literature.

fun_facts.text: The Library cites rival authors such as Panyasis and Pherecydes, showing that Greek myths had many variants.

language_notes.text: "Wroth" is an archaic word for angry; "quitted" means left.
The rock's name Laughless recalls Demeter's grief at her daughter's loss; the place was linked to Eleusinian cult tradition.
"Crone" means an old woman; "bade" is the past tense of bid, meaning invited.
The Thesmophoria was an Athenian women's festival honouring Demeter, in which ritual joking was customary, said here to echo Iambe's jests.
"Of nights" means during the nights; "stripped off its mortal flesh" means burned away the mortal part so the child would become immortal.
Praxithea appears abruptly without introduction; she is presumably the child's mother, and the text elsewhere gives Metanira this role. The pronoun "him" is Demophon.
"The Maid" translates Kore, a title for Persephone; "tarry" means linger.

context_notes.text: Pluto is lord of the underworld and brother of Zeus, who is Persephone's father; Zeus's complicity is part of the story.
Triptolemus became the hero who spread agriculture, a gift of Demeter, from Eleusis to the world.
Acheron is a river of the underworld; Ascalaphus was punished for betraying Persephone's act of eating.

literary_notes.text: Demeter's tireless torchlit search and angry departure from heaven show a determined, passionate mother-goddess who puts her grief above her divine duties.
The nightly fire treatment, performed in secret, prepares for the interruption that will ruin the attempt.
Praxithea's cry of alarm, meant to protect the child, destroys his chance at immortality.
Persephone eats the seed without foreseeing the consequence, and that small act binds her to the underworld.
